passage: I watched my cousin Zubin bargain with his mother about phone time last Sunday, and I was surprised because he stayed calm. Last month he used to argue until doors banged. This time he said, "Amma, can we try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks? If I keep my marks up and you see me put it away at nine, we can talk about more." His mother looked at him a long moment. "Two weeks," she said. "Show me." He did not sulk or promise the moon. I can't tell what he felt, maybe nervous, maybe just tired of fighting. Later he told me it felt good to be trusted a little. Ritu.

qa.q: What did Zubin ask his mother for?
qa.a: He asked to try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling as he made his proposal?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous and hopeful, and perhaps tired of arguing. Ritu admits not being certain, since he stayed calm on the outside.

qa.q: What made Zubin's approach more likely to succeed?
qa.a: He offered trust-building steps and a trial period, instead of arguing or demanding.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother have felt hearing it?
qa.a: She may have felt reassured that he was thinking about responsibility, while still wanting to see it work. 🙂

grounding: A teen bargains calmly for phone time with a trial period, seen by an observer.

passage:
Friday. Afreen wanted to stay out until ten for her friend's engagement dinner and argued with her father, Jagdish, for twenty minutes. He said no, she stormed off. 
Sunday. She wrote out a plan: the venue, who would drive her home, a message every hour, and "if I break any of it, I'll go back to nine." She left it by his tea.
Thursday. Jagdish said, "We'll try ten for this dinner only." Afreen said thank you and kept every promise. A few weeks later, when she asked for another late evening, he said yes before she'd finished asking.

qa.q: What did Afreen leave by her father's tea?
qa.a: She left a written plan by his tea.

qa.q: Why did Afreen write out a plan instead of arguing again?
qa.a: She probably realised that arguing had not worked, and she wanted to show him she could be trusted. Writing it also gave her a calmer way to ask.

qa.q: What did the trial arrangement do for the family?
qa.a: It gave Jagdish a way to say yes safely, and gave Afreen a chance to prove herself.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt on Friday?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and firm, and perhaps annoyed by the argument, since he said no and she stormed off.

grounding: A teen negotiates curfew with a written plan and a trial period, across several days.

passage:
Hansa, you want to cycle to the lake with your friends and your mother says no? Let me tell you how your Disha Masi got her cycle.
When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, I wanted to ride to school alone. My father said no, every time. I argued, I sulked, and once I even took the cycle without asking. Big mistake. He locked it for a month.
So I tried a different way. I wrote down a plan. Same road every day, the main one, not the shortcut. I'd call from the school phone when I reached. And we'd try it for two weeks. If I missed one call, the cycle went back in the shed.
I showed it to him after dinner, calmly, no crying. He read it twice. "Two weeks," he said.
I didn't miss a single call. After two weeks he said, "Take the shortcut if you like."

qa.q: How long was the trial period in Disha's plan?
qa.a: They'd try it for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Disha's father likely feeling when he read the plan twice?
qa.a: He was probably cautious but reassured, since the calm, written plan showed he could trust Disha after the earlier sneaking.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Disha Masi's story?
qa.a: Switching from arguing and sneaking to a calm, written plan with a two-week trial and daily calls, which built trust.

qa.q: How might Disha's father have felt when she took the cycle without asking?
qa.a: He probably felt worried and betrayed, which is why he locked it away for a month.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager negotiating independence with trust-building steps and a trial period, after arguing and sneaking failed.

passage:
Anirban's father, Shankar, came home from a twelve-hour night shift at the bus depot, and Anirban had been waiting all morning to talk about phone time. The flat was small, his little sister was practising harmonium, and his father's eyes were red.
Anirban almost started with, "Everyone else gets two hours!" He stopped. Not now. Not like that.
He waited till his father had eaten and slept a little. Then, at four, he brought a cup of tea and a page from his notebook.
"Baba, can I suggest something? One hour on weekdays, only after homework. Phone stays in the kitchen at night. You can check the homework. Let's try it for a month. If marks drop, we go back."
Shankar read it slowly, sipping the tea. "You wrote this yourself?"
"Yes."
"One month," he said. "And the phone charges next to mine."

qa.q: How long was Shankar's night shift?
qa.a: It was a twelve-hour night shift at the bus depot.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he almost said "Everyone else gets two hours"?
qa.a: Anirban felt impatient and frustrated after waiting all morning, but recognised that arguing now would fail.

qa.q: What made Anirban's proposal likely to succeed?
qa.a: He chose a calm moment, offered clear limits the father could check, and suggested a one-month trial with a way back if marks dropped.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when he saw the tea and the written page?
qa.a: He probably felt pleasantly surprised and respected, which made him more willing to agree.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager negotiating phone time with calm, trust-building steps and a trial period, under a tired-parent constraint.

passage:
Siddharth wanted to play Saturday football at the big ground in Andheri, forty minutes away by metro. His friend Kunal had solved the same problem by telling his parents he was at tuition. He'd been caught in the second week and banned from going anywhere.
Siddharth didn't want that. On Thursday he found his father, Mridul, fixing a shelf.
"Papa, can I show you a plan for Saturdays?"
He had it on his phone: metro both ways with two friends, location sharing on, a call when he reached, home by seven-thirty. "Let's try four Saturdays. If I'm late once, we stop and talk again."
Mridul put the screwdriver down. "And if the metro's delayed?"
"I'll call before seven-thirty, not after."
His father thought for a long time. "Four Saturdays. First one, I'll drop you and pick you up."
"Deal," Siddharth said.

qa.q: How far was the big ground by metro?
qa.a: It was forty minutes away by metro.

qa.q: What was Mridul probably thinking when he asked about metro delays?
qa.a: He was probably cautious and worried about safety, testing whether Siddharth had thought the plan through.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth's approach work better than Kunal's?
qa.a: Siddharth offered a calm plan with check-ins and a four-week trial, which built trust, while Kunal's sneaking got him caught and banned.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel hearing about Siddharth's Saturdays?
qa.a: Kunal might feel regretful or envious, seeing that honesty and a plan got Siddharth what sneaking lost him.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager negotiating independence with trust-building steps and a trial period, contrasted with a friend who sneaked.

passage:
"Papa, can we talk about the phone rule? Properly, not shouting."
Anand looked up from the newspaper. "Last time 'properly' ended with a door slam."
"I know. Sorry for that. Here's my idea. Right now the phone goes to the hall at nine. I want it till ten-thirty on school nights."
"And you'll be up till two."
"That's why I'm offering this: at ten-thirty it goes on the hall charger, and I put it there myself. You don't have to ask."
"And if it doesn't?"
"Then it's back to nine, no argument. Two-week trial. You can check the screen-time page every Sunday."
Anand folded the paper. "Why ten-thirty?"
"The group study call goes till ten. I've been missing the last hour, and then sneaking the phone back from the hall to catch up."
"You've been sneaking it?"
"Yes, Papa. I'd rather not have to."
A long pause. "Two weeks. Hall charger. I'm checking on Sundays, Irfan."
"Deal."

qa.q: Till what time does the group study call go?
qa.a: The group study call goes till ten.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when admitting to sneaking the phone?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt nervous and a bit ashamed saying it, but also wanted to be trusted; the admission may also have been a way to show honesty.

qa.q: Which part of Irfan's proposal made it easier to say yes?
qa.a: A clear two-week trial with a built-in consequence, putting the phone on the hall charger unasked and Sunday checks, gave Anand ways to build trust. 👍

qa.q: How might Anand have felt hearing about the sneaking?
qa.a: Anand may have felt surprised and a little hurt, but the honest admission next to a calm plan likely made the trial feel safer to agree to.

grounding: It shows a teenager negotiating phone time with a parent by offering trust-building steps and a trial period instead of arguing or sneaking.
